title: "I am near"
hookLine: when my servants ask about Me, I am near, I answer (2:186)
tomorrow: Good in this world and the next
last: HAMM — THE DU'A AND THE DOCTOR.

cards: On a bad phone line, people raise their voices. Across a parking lot, they shout and wave. To someone right beside them, in the dark at the end of a long day, they whisper.
The volume of a voice carries a guess about distance: how far away the listener is. So here's a question for anyone who has ever prayed, or wanted to: how far away is the One you're talking to?

teach.b: The answer is in Surah al-Baqarah, verse one hundred eighty-six, tucked in the middle of the verses about the Ramadan fast. And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh.

I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me. Commentators point to how that verse is built. Elsewhere in the Qur'an, when people ask the Prophet a question, the answer begins with one word: Say.
They ask you about the new moons; say. They ask you about wine; say. But here, when they ask about Allah Himself, there's no say.

The answer comes straight back: I am near. The Prophet ﷺ taught the same thing on a road. Bukhari and Muslim report that on a journey, the companions were calling out Allahu akbar at the tops of their voices.
He told them: go easy on yourselves.
You're not calling on someone deaf or absent. You're calling on One who hears, who is near, and who is with you.
A verse in Surah Qaf puts it even closer: We are nearer to him than his jugular vein. The vein in your own neck. So in Islam you'll often see du'a made quietly, lips moving, almost no sound.

teach.h: YOU DON'T SHOUT AT SOMEONE THAT CLOSE.
teach.b: Not because anything is secret, but because you don't shout at someone who's that close. Nearness here isn't a feeling you have to work up. It's a claim the text makes, whether you feel it or not.

how: Muslims often make du'a quietly, with the lips moving and little sound, following 2:186 and the Prophet's teaching that Allah is near and hears.

o: a vein in the wrist where the pulse is felt
the neck vein God is said to be nearer than
a vein in the arm where blood is drawn

games.q: what's inside "I am near" — tap the pairs.
p: not calling someone deaf or absent

s: 2:186 sits in the middle of the verses about fasting
it's tucked among the Ramadan verses of Surah al-Baqarah (2:183–187).
the verse begins with 'say', like other answers to questions
that's what's surprising: when they ask about Allah, the answer comes with no 'say'.
the Prophet ﷺ told the companions to call out louder
he told them to go easy: they were calling One who hears, is near, and is with them.

games.q: you're on a journey with the companions, and everyone is shouting Allahu akbar at the top of their lungs. what does the Prophet ﷺ say?
o: louder, so the whole valley hears
go easy: you're calling One who is near
games.why: he said they weren't calling someone deaf or absent, but One who hears, who is near and with them (Bukhari, Muslim).

practice: Find the pulse in your neck, if you can, or at your wrist, and bring to mind the thing you asked for two days ago, or anything you'd like to ask.
If you pray, say it, but barely: lips moving, almost no sound, as if to someone sitting right beside you; if you don't, whisper it to yourself just as quietly. Then stay in the quiet after it.

wordCard.voice: Jugular vein. The nearness verse in Surah Qaf says God is nearer to a person than this, the vein in their own neck.

orig.note: Arabic: then surely I am near, from 2:186.

carryVoice: Your line: he is near. Nearer than the vein in your own neck. That's day one hundred thirty-two.

sources.q: And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me.
We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2992; Sahih Muslim 2704 (you are not calling one deaf or absent)
